The villa I am staying in at Samujana on the Thai resort island of Koh Samui – and which comes with a $US2.35 million ($2,938,000) price tag – has a gym, luxurious home cinema, four bedrooms and a small team of staff to attend to my every whim. But despite the remarkable inclusions I find myself spending most of my time simply lolling about in its infinity-edge pool.

The view from the pool, it must be said, is mesmerising: a coastline of beaches with swaying palms and smooth rocky outcrops in the distance. In the foreground are the luxuriant gardens of this 27-villa development, terraced down a gently sloping 7.2-hectare site.

It is also invitingly close to several other “lolling about” spots in the villa designed by Bali-based architect Garry Fell.

Fell’s Gfab Architects studio is renowned for its style of tropical architecture that combines modernist lines and an open design.

How it started

Samujana had its beginnings in 2005 when a group of expats, led by British couple Gerry and John Kinder, developed a series of villas for their families. Today it is managed by a professional team led by Swiss-born Richard Meir, who has managed some of Asia’s most exclusive resorts.

It is a place where you can do as little or as much as you like with in-house Thai-cooking lessons, chefs and bespoke boating trips all available, and organised through your dedicated villa manager. This makes the property attractive for own-use and rentals.

Samujana’s property sales manager Diah Intan Maulidya says the development has attracted Australian buyers and there is a growing number of Chinese buyers showing interest.

Along with Villa 7, there are four villas completed in 2015 that are currently on the market. They range from a four-bedroom villa for $US3 million through to a six-bedroom villa at $US5 million.

Can Australians buy in?

Current Thai law does not allow foreign ownership of freehold land. Instead, buyers in the Samujana Estate can hold the properties under an initial 30-year lease and then renew the lease for two further periods of 30 years – effectively giving a 90-year lease. The Samujana Estate is marketed by its own villa sales division.

For further information see samujana.com or email property_sales@samujana.com

A quintessential Pittwater pad, this generous family home occupies a 1317-square-metre waterfront lot gazing west across the water to the national park. The five-level residence has wide inviting verandahs and a suspended pool taking in the stunning view. The property also includes a boat house and self-contained studio.

Tell us about your local market.

Although my office is based in Toorak, for Sotheby’s and for me personally, it’s not about being suburb-specific. It comes down to connections with your clients.

What can your clients expect from listing with you?

My biggest strength is my ability to build relationships. I’ve sold for people three or four times, and seven times for one client. I don’t dress conservatively either. Leather pants, pink furs – I create a point of difference.

What has been one of your most memorable sales?

I’ve just had the best five days of my career, selling just under $24 million.

What would you change about the industry if you could?

There just aren’t enough women in real estate, especially at the top end.

Were you ever on a different career path?

I was actually a snowboarding instructor in Whistler for a couple of years.

The rise of apartment living is often discussed as a modern phenomenon in Australia, but there are pockets in our major cities which house long-established buildings that have epitomised glamorous living for years. The Macleay Regis apartment building, in Macleay Street in Sydney’s Potts Point, is such a building.

An iconic landmark, its gorgeous art deco features, grand entrance lobby and luxurious finishes over nine storeys attracted the cream of Australian society when it was built in 1939.

In the massive penthouse lived Harold Christmas, one of the founders of the Woolworths empire, who commissioned the tower from well-known architects Pitt & Phillips on a design inspired by New York’s Rockefeller building. He had it built on the site of two original houses in Elizabeth Bay.

“And it’s still an amazing penthouse today,” says Victoria Morish, related by marriage to the Christmas family, whose own parents became only the third owners, buying it from legendary radio presenter Grace Gibbons.

“It used to be the whole top floor but has since been divided into two, with my parents’ penthouse by far the bigger one.”

That grand 350-square-metre penthouse above 12 Macleay Street, with views from the Harbour Bridge to The Heads, is on the market.

It follows the death of Morish’s father, the much-awarded gynaecologist Professor Malcolm Coppleson. His late wife, Patricia, a model he met in London when he helped her after a fall from the step of a bus, later became

Vogue’s editor-at-large.

Their son Mark Coppleson, Morish’s brother, says it was a tough decision to sell. “It’s just got an incredible feel about it,” he says.

Certainly one of the grandest of apartment blocks to be built in Sydney during the inter-war years, Macleay Regis originally had a kitchen on the eighth floor from which waitresses would travel in a service lift delivering meals to residents. Its laundry and drying room was the first in Sydney to have coin-slot-operated washing machines, while it also had a full concierge service.

The penthouse is palatial in size and ambience, with soaring ceilings, cypress parquet flooring, a baronial dining room panelled in oak, and a vast living room with a stone fireplace. It leads to a sheltered north-east-facing rooftop garden with majestic views, yes, befitting a king.

Stewart Pickering moved from Mosman to Maleny in the 1970s and hasn’t looked back. The owner of the Maleny Hotel for nearly 20 years before selling in 1996, Stewart and his wife Gretel have thrived in a community he describes as dedicated and welcoming.

“I had been to the Sunshine Coast on holidays and seen the enormous potential of the area,” he says. “To borrow a description from [demographer] Bernard Salt, Maleny is a lifestyle town for older people.”

Green change opportunity

Of the 3734 people who call Maleny home, 45 per cent are aged 60 and over but Ray White Maleny agent Rebecca Rea says the town is also popular with professional couples wanting to make a green change.

“You can work from home, or it’s only 70 minutes from Brisbane, so the city is still accessible,” says Rea.

“It’s possible to buy big homes on smaller lots that you can lock up and leave, or acreages for hobby farming. A lot of people move from interstate looking for space and the chance to grow vegies and keep chooks.”

You won’t have to give up good food and coffee either. Maleny has more than its fair share of cafes, many of which you’ll find along vibrant Maple Street.

There’s also top-quality gelato (made from award-winning local milk) and a host of fabulous cheeses at Maleny Food Co. Local restaurants offer cuisine from as far afield as Nepal, Thailand and Europe.

The eco-conscious community offers organic produce, farmers’ markets and workshops in permaculture, plus it’s a haven for artists and craftspeople whose wares can be found in galleries and boutiques.

Ideal for nature lovers

Celebrated for its natural beauty, Maleny is set on the eastern slopes of the Blackall Range overlooking the Glass House Mountains, which means nature lovers are spoilt for choice when it comes to the great outdoors.

The district is home to the Mary Cairncross Scenic Reserve, a 55-hectare remnant of the rainforest that once covered the entire range.

From the new Rainforest Discovery Centre you can venture out along walking trails and learn about the diverse animal and plant life of the region.

Maleny’s Botanic Gardens and Bird World is a top spot for a Devonshire tea with a view, while the more adventurous can swim under the waterfall at Gardners Falls, or kayak across the Baroon Pocket Dam, which also offers fishing, picnicking and bushwalking.

I used to frequent St Canice’s Church in Sydney’s Elizabeth Bay for their Sunday Mass. The congregation was a diverse but harmonious group. At that time, the priest used to let the homeless, from neighbouring Kings Cross, sleep in the covered entry and some of these “residents” would also turn up for Mass. Alongside them were some of the most elegant older ladies I have ever seen, beautifully dressed with hats and matching handbags and shoes. I soon discovered that many of these women were long-time residents of the stately apartment buildings in Elizabeth Bay and nearby Potts Point. Our feature story looks at one of the most famous of these grand buildings, the Macleay Regis, and highlights the penthouse that is now for sale in the building. It is as gracious and as timeless as its residents, past and present.

Ah, the blessed bliss of brand blindness. Perhaps it is only a child who can greet a ride in a Ferrari with a shrug and a demand for an iPad to cure the boredom. Or perhaps it’s only my children, otherwise lovely miniature people, who can so thoroughly fail to appreciate the wizardry of the Italian engineers who came up with the GTC4 Lusso.

This, clearly, is a Ferrari for people who already have a Ferrari (a proper one, with two seats and the engine behind your ears), but have made the all-too-common error of having children and discovered they need more space.

Somehow, despite having four seats and

all-wheel-drive, like a typical family car, the engineers managed to make the Lusso, priced at $578,000, invigorating as well as practical.

A giant V12 engine (making 507kW and 697Nm) that can hurl you – and the temporary contents of your children’s stomachs – from 0 to 100km/h in 3.4 seconds, on your way to a top speed of 335km/h, is a big help. What’s not helpful is the passenger screen that sat right in front of my wife, not only allowing her to control the music, but displaying for her in lurid detail exactly how unnecessarily fast we were going. This is possibly the most ill-advised invention since online shopping.

However, Ferrari has somehow managed to make a vehicle this big look like a sexy super car. This is a spectacular achievement. It’s also quite stunning to drive, and makes just enough noise to drown out the complaints from the back seats. And the passenger one.

I think they were shouting “Low down!” but I still can’t work out why.

Pharmacare’s owner Toby Browne and his wife Julie have returned their home redesign project in Newport on Sydney’s northern beaches to the market with a $4.5 million asking price.

The founder of the vitamin giant has long shown a penchant for the work of architect Mark Hurcum, who redesigned the property following the Brownes’ purchase in 2006 for $1.7 million.

Now a five-bedroom home with fancy waterfront facilities (think boat shed, pontoon and slipway), it was first shown to the market in February with $5 million hopes but returns for spring with a revised guide of $4.5 million through Josephine Cowling of LJ Hooker Mona Vale.

China’s appetite for Australian-made vitamins in recent years has been good news for another Newport local, Marcus Blackmore. Having debuted on the Forbes rich list last year, the vitamin mogul paid $9.25 million a year ago for the Bayview waterfront property Sandgate amid plans by his wife Caroline to remodel it.

Prominent Brisbane developer Frank Hallam and his wife Lynne have sold their luxurious Hamilton Queenslander after more than one year on the market.

Hallam, who owns Hemmant Constructions, held strong on his price after first listing it in June last year and finally achieved a record-breaking price for the suburb, fetching $7.6 million.

The home has seven bedrooms, a bowling alley and a 1000-bottle wine cellar.

The Hallams bought the property for $3.5 million in June 2007. They spent two years in council and construction and 18 months digging the block. The house was moved four times before it was placed in its current position.

Ray White New Farm principal Matt Lancashire brokered the deal but wouldn’t comment on the details of the sale.

Former Carlton Football Club vice president and director of entertainment business Event, Richard Newton, and his wife, Liz, are selling a luxury apartment in Ubertas’ 505 St Kilda Road.

The sixth-floor apartment stretches the length of the complex, capturing views over the treetops of St Kilda Road and Fawkner Park. It has five bedrooms and two family-sized kitchens.

The Karl Fender designed complex replaced what was said to be St Kilda Road’s first high-rise office building, developed in the 1960s.

Kay & Burton’s Nicole Gleeson, who is marketing the apartment, is expecting a price of between $6.5 million and $7.15 million.
